# Overview: What the skin microbiome is and why “commensal vs pathogen” is a spectrum

The skin hosts diverse microbial communities that occupy moist, sebaceous, and dry microenvironments and include bacteria, fungi, viruses, and microeukaryotes; by definition, “commensals” are microbes with neutral or beneficial interactions with the host, while “pathogens” cause disease, though many taxa straddle a continuum depending on context and host state <cite id="690189ba-1">Across the moist, sebaceous, or dry microenvironments of the skin are distinct microbial communities encompassing bacteria, fungi, viruses, and microeukaryotes… members are referred to as skin commensals, which we define as microorganisms whose interactions on the skin are either neutral or beneficial</cite>. Skin colonization is shaped by site-specific pH, moisture, salinity, and sebum, as well as genotype, age, and sex, with early studies already listing Staphylococcus, Propionibacterium (now Cutibacterium), Micrococcus, and Corynebacterium among abundant genera <cite id="690189ba-0">Abundant bacterial genera on the surface layers of the human skin include Staphylococcus, Propionibacterium, Micrococcus, and Corynebacterium… composition varies with body site (pH, moisture, salinity, sebum) and factors such as genotype, age, and sex</cite>. The skin microbiome is an active participant in barrier integrity, modulating inflammation, promoting epidermal differentiation, and enhancing wound healing, while also protecting against invaders via competitive exclusion and direct antimicrobial metabolites; yet its role is context dependent, shifting between health and disease with ecological change <cite id="690189ba-1">Members of the skin microbiome are not merely hitchhikers… modulate the cutaneous inflammatory response, promotion of epidermal differentiation, and enhancement of wound healing… occupation of skin niches provides protection by competitive exclusion and microbiome-derived antimicrobial molecules; the role of commensals is context dependent</cite>.

# Composition: Which bacteria typically dominate and where

Habitat dictates taxa: lipid-rich sebaceous areas favor Propionibacterium/Cutibacterium and Staphylococcus, whereas drier sites harbor more Corynebacterium and Bacilli; phyla commonly include Firmicutes and Actinobacteria, with regional shifts across body sites <cite id="690189ba-0">Abundant bacterial genera… include Staphylococcus, Propionibacterium, Micrococcus, and Corynebacterium</cite><cite id="690189ba-2">Skin microbiome bacteria are mostly from Firmicutes, Actinobacteria, Bacteroidetes, and Proteobacteria… variation in temperature, moisture, and pH favors survival of some bacteria over others</cite>. In disease, dysbiosis often features reduced lipophilic taxa (Cutibacterium/Propionibacterium) and altered proportions of Corynebacterium and Streptococcus, with decreased diversity and shifts among phyla observed in psoriatic lesions compared with healthy skin <cite id="690189ba-2">Analysis of the skin microbiome in psoriatic plaques… a decrease in microbial diversity… variation in relative abundance of Firmicutes, Actinobacteria, and Proteobacteria with a prevalence of Firmicutes and lower level of Actinobacteria… decreased representation of Cutibacterium and Lactobacilli; increased Corynebacterium associated with inflammation severity; increased Streptococcus; Staphylococcus epidermidis more common in normal skin</cite>. More broadly, commensals can prevent colonization by pathogens via niche competition and immune priming, and colonization with particular species (e.g., S. epidermidis, S. aureus, Corynebacterium pseudodiphtheriticum, Cutibacterium acnes) alters innate immune “alarmins” and T-cell profiles in skin <cite id="690189ba-0">Commensal bacteria can passively occupy a similar ecological niche to a pathogenic microbe, thus impeding its skin colonization… commensal bacteria… can selectively induce antimicrobial peptides production and provide a protective effect in vivo when administered before infectious challenge</cite><cite id="f14b695c-0">Colonization with commensal species… upregulates IL-17A and IFN-γ–expressing T cells and S100A8 and S100A6… commensal colonization is crucial protection against invasive microbes</cite>.

# Characteristics of commensal skin bacteria

Commensal Staphylococcus epidermidis is abundant and immunomodulatory: it activates γδ T cells and induces antimicrobial perforin-2, promotes regulatory T-cell tolerance in early life, and can skew toward Th17 inflammation if neonatal colonization is by S. aureus rather than S. epidermidis; importantly, S. epidermidis-induced T cells accelerate wound healing and enhance killing of intracellular S. aureus in ex vivo human skin, while its lipoteichoic acid (LTA) activates TLR2 on keratinocytes to mitigate inflammation and support barrier function <cite id="f14b695c-0">Staphylococcus epidermidis has been shown to activate gamma delta T cells and induce antimicrobial perforin-2… early life colonization with S. epidermidis promotes activation of regulatory T cells… neonatal colonization with S. aureus upregulates IL-1β and increases Th17:Treg ratio… commensal colonization leads to accumulation of IL-17A and IFN-γ–expressing T cells and upregulates S100A8 and S100A6… T cells induced by S. epidermidis accelerate wound healing… Staphylococcus epidermidis produces lipoteichoic acid (LTA) that activates TLR2 and exerts anti-inflammatory effects on keratinocytes</cite><cite id="690189ba-3">Staphylococcus epidermidis… triggers AMP expression by keratinocytes, and LTA produced by S. epidermidis mitigates cutaneous inflammation through TLR2 signaling</cite>. Mechanistically, S. epidermidis contributes to homeostasis by stimulating β-defensin secretion from keratinocytes, producing phenol-soluble modulin peptides that inhibit S. aureus, secreting a serine protease that inhibits S. aureus biofilm formation, and releasing LTA that represses keratinocyte inflammatory cytokines—properties that argue against broad-spectrum antibiotic targeting and motivate strategies that preserve commensal colonization while reducing pathogen load <cite id="f14b695c-3">Staphylococcus epidermidis… stimulates secretion of antimicrobial peptide β-defensin from keratinocytes, a phenol-soluble modulin that inhibits S. aureus, a serine protease that inhibits S. aureus biofilm, and lipoteichoic acid that represses inflammatory cytokine release from keratinocytes</cite><cite id="f14b695c-4">S. epidermidis inhibits S. aureus growth in lesions by stimulating AMP production through TLR2, and by phenol-soluble modulins and bacteriocins that act synergically against S. aureus and S. pyogenes; S. epidermidis can inhibit biofilm formation by S. aureus, and its LTA shows immunomodulatory properties in healing wounds</cite><cite id="690189ba-0">Recent surveys… established that the skin microbiota plays a beneficial role… bacteria present on our skin have similar functions in immune regulation and disease pathogenesis</cite>. S. epidermidis also produces broad-spectrum bacteriocins, exemplified by epidermicin from a nasal isolate, underscoring its direct antimicrobial arsenal on skin <cite id="f14b695c-1">Staphylococcus epidermidis produces diverse, therapeutically relevant bacteriocins… S. epidermidis B273 contains a plasmid with the biosynthetic gene cluster for epidermicin NI01, a broad-spectrum type II antimicrobial peptide</cite>.

Cutibacterium/Propionibacterium and Corynebacterium species are hallmark commensals of sebaceous and dry skin, respectively, with lipid dependence and biofilm-like associations to follicles and stratum corneum; they contribute to immune homeostasis via microbiota-derived antimicrobial molecules and competitive exclusion, while their abundance can drop with barrier compromise and dysbiosis <cite id="690189ba-1">Occupation of skin niches by the microbiome provides protection against invading pathogens by competitive exclusion and by biosynthesis of microbiome-derived antimicrobial molecules</cite><cite id="690189ba-2">There was a decreased representation of Cutibacterium in psoriatic skin and increased Corynebacterium associated with disease severity</cite><cite id="690189ba-0">Early studies showed that abundant bacterial genera on the skin include Staphylococcus, Propionibacterium, Micrococcus, and Corynebacterium</cite>. Commensal microbes produce bioactive metabolites that kill pathogens and stimulate keratinocytes and immune cells, shaping innate and adaptive responses and maintaining tolerance; keratinocytes sense microbes through PRRs recognizing flagellin and LPS (Gram−), and peptidoglycan and LTA (Gram+), triggering AMP secretion and activation of epidermal and dermal immune cells <cite id="690189ba-3">Commensal microbes produce bioactive metabolites that kill pathogens and stimulate keratinocytes and immune cells… keratinocytes sample the microbiota through PRRs that recognize PAMPs such as flagellin and LPS… and peptidoglycan and lipoteichoic acid… inducing secretion of antimicrobial peptides and immune mediators by keratinocytes, and activation of epidermal and dermal immune cells</cite>. In aging and disease, diversity declines and commensal predominance wanes, reflecting changing skin physiology and immune homeostasis <cite id="690189ba-1">In aging individuals… changes to the skin are concomitant with changes to the microbiome and a loss of phylogenetic diversity</cite><cite id="690189ba-2">A decrease of commensal bacteria and the increase of non-commensal species could alter skin immune homeostasis, favoring inflammatory responses and impaired barrier functions</cite>.

# Characteristics of pathogenic and problematic (opportunistic) bacteria

Staphylococcus aureus, including methicillin-resistant strains, is a potent skin colonizer and pathogen whose presence increases inflammatory responses in skin, contrasting with coagulase-negative congeners that are usually benign; manipulating their relative abundance thus modulates cutaneous immunity and disease risk <cite id="f14b695c-2">Colonization by Staphylococcus aureus, a well-known pathogen, increases inflammatory responses within the skin; colonization by Staphylococcus epidermis can be innocuous or beneficial… manipulating the abundance of these two species likely alters the skin microbiome and modulates cutaneous immune response</cite>. Mechanistically, S. aureus produces toxins and proteases that disrupt the epidermal barrier and aggravate inflammation; notably, sapienic (C16:1 cis) and palmitoleic (C16:1 trans) fatty acids in sebum exhibit selective antibacterial activity against S. aureus, and lower sapienic acid levels and inverse correlations with S. aureus abundance are observed in atopic dermatitis, supporting a barrier–microbiome inflammatory loop <cite id="f14b695c-3">Staphylococcus aureus… produces several toxins and proteases, which aggravate skin inflammation by disrupting the epidermal barrier… sapienic acid and palmitoleic acid possess selective antibacterial activity against S. aureus; sapienic acid is present in human sebum, is lower in atopic dermatitis, and inversely correlated with S. aureus abundance</cite>. In atopic dermatitis lesions, coagulase-negative Staphylococcus can inhibit S. aureus growth through TLR2-stimulated AMPs, PSMs, and bacteriocins, and S. epidermidis specifically inhibits S. aureus biofilm formation, underscoring interspecies antagonism in disease sites <cite id="f14b695c-4">S. epidermidis inhibits S. aureus growth in lesions via TLR2-mediated AMP stimulation and secretion of phenol-soluble modulins and bacteriocins; S. epidermidis can inhibit S. aureus biofilm</cite>. By analogy, Gram-positive pathogens like Corynebacterium diphtheriae inhabit skin and mucosa and cause diphtheria, illustrating the broader category of exogenous bacterial pathogens that breach tolerance and induce systemic inflammation; in skin ecosystems, shifts toward gram-negative taxa can mirror dysbiosis with heightened inflammatory gene signatures <cite id="690189ba-3">Skin resident microbes play an important role… Disruptions in skin microbial communities may contribute to triggering skin autoimmune diseases</cite><cite id="690189ba-4">Johnson et al. discovered substantial changes in skin microbial composition, with decreased lipophilic taxa (Propionibacterium) and increased gram-negative taxa (Burkholderia, Citrobacter, and Vibrio); skin microbial dysbiosis is associated with an increased inflammatory gene signature</cite>.

# How the microbiome influences the immune system

Commensal microbes educate and calibrate skin immunity. During early life, specific colonizers imprint tolerance and homeostasis: neonatal S. epidermidis colonization promotes regulatory T cells and tolerance, whereas neonatal S. aureus colonization skews toward IL-1β and Th17 dominance, demonstrating a window for immune set-pointing by the microbiome <cite id="f14b695c-0">Early life colonization of skin with Staphylococcus epidermidis promotes activation of regulatory T cells in neonatal skin… neonatal colonization with Staphylococcus aureus upregulates IL-1β and increases the ratio of Th17 cells to Tregs</cite>. Dendritic cells sample commensal antigens and present them to T cells in neonatal skin, a process critical for tolerance; reduced commensals and increased non-commensals disrupt homeostasis, biasing toward inflammation and barrier impairment <cite id="690189ba-2">Skin dendritic cells can present antigens from skin microbiota and that this mechanism, in neonatal life, is essential to correctly develop tolerance to commensals; decrease of commensal bacteria and the increase of non-commensal species could alter immune homeostasis, favoring inflammatory responses and impaired barrier functions</cite>. Commensal signals engage multiple sentinel pathways: keratinocyte PRRs sense microbial PAMPs (flagellin, LPS, peptidoglycan, LTA) to elicit AMPs and cytokines, and TLR2 engagement by S. epidermidis LTA mitigates cutaneous inflammation, coupling microbial sensing to barrier-stabilizing immune programs <cite id="690189ba-3">Keratinocytes sample the microbiota through PRRs that recognize PAMPs… inducing secretion of antimicrobial peptides and immune mediators… Staphylococcus epidermidis, a skin commensal, triggers AMP expression by keratinocytes, and LTA… mitigates cutaneous inflammation through TLR2 signaling</cite>. γδ T cells and perforin-2–producing immunity are induced by commensal staphylococci and contribute to pathogen control and wound healing, while commensal-driven alarmins (S100A8/A6) and chemokines link innate and adaptive responses in a way that enhances host defense without wholesale inflammation <cite id="f14b695c-0">Staphylococcus epidermidis has been shown to activate gamma delta T cells and induce perforin-2… accumulation of IL-17A and IFN-γ–expressing T cells in skin with commensal colonization upregulates S100A8 and S100A6</cite>.

Pathogenic or dysbiotic microbiota, by contrast, bias immunity toward inflammation and tissue disruption. Cutibacterium acnes/Propionibacterium acnes strains can drive mixed Th1/Th17 responses via sebocyte and immune signaling (IL-6, IL-1β, TGF-β), with elevated IL-17 in acne lesions and synergy among IL-17, TNF-α, and IL-1 to induce metalloproteinases and further inflammation; some studies show increased serum IL-17 in acne patients and robust Th17 responses to acne strains relative to healthy donors <cite id="a44049b3-0">Cutibacterium acnes can promote mixed Th17/Th1 responses by inducing IL-17A and IFN-γ; IL-17/IL-22 promote AMPs; sebocytes stimulated by Cutibacterium acnes promote Th17 activation via IL-6, IL-1β, and TGF-β; serum IL-17 is increased in acne scarring; IL-17 expression in PBMCs is significantly increased in acne skin with acne strains</cite><cite id="a44049b3-2">IL-17, TNF-α, and IL-1 synergize in acne by inducing metalloproteinases; serum IL-17 is increased in acne vulgaris scarring compared to those without</cite><cite id="a44049b3-3">Propionibacterium acnes is a potent inducer of Th17 and Th1, but not Th2 responses; IL-17-expressing cells are present in acne skin but not normal donors; vitamin A and D inhibit P. acnes–induced Th17 differentiation</cite><cite id="a44049b3-4">IL-17 levels are elevated in acne lesions with IL-6, IL-23, TGF-β, and other mediators; Cutibacterium acnes can trigger IL-17 and IFN-γ; PBMCs exposed to Propionibacterium acnes produce IL-1β, IL-6, IL-12, and IL-23, polarizing T cells to Th1/Th17</cite>. S. aureus colonization elevates IL-1β and Th17/Treg imbalance and disrupts the epidermal barrier via toxins and proteases, connecting immune activation to impaired barrier function and chronic inflammation, as seen in atopic dermatitis, where commensals counterbalance S. aureus through AMPs, bacteriocins, and biofilm inhibition <cite id="f14b695c-0">Neonatal colonization with S. aureus upregulates IL-1β and increases the ratio of Th17 cells to Tregs</cite><cite id="f14b695c-3">S. aureus produces toxins and proteases that aggravate skin inflammation by disrupting the epidermal barrier</cite><cite id="f14b695c-4">S. epidermidis inhibits S. aureus growth and biofilm via TLR2-mediated AMPs, PSMs, and bacteriocins</cite>. In systemic and connective-tissue disease contexts, reduced lipophilic taxa and increased gram-negative invaders correlate with heightened inflammatory signatures in skin, consistent with a microbial trigger for immune dysregulation and tissue remodeling <cite id="690189ba-4">Decreased lipophilic taxa (Propionibacterium) and increased gram-negative taxa (Burkholderia, Citrobacter, Vibrio) in SSc skin; dysbiosis is associated with increased inflammatory gene signatures</cite>.

# Barrier–microbiome–immune cross-talk in disease

Barrier disruption creates a permissive environment for dysbiosis and infection. Loss of barrier integrity—whether from immune disease, radiation, or aging—allows pathogen ingress and shifts microbiome composition, with reduced Cutibacterium, increased gram-negatives, and elevated inflammatory gene signatures; conversely, commensal-driven AMPs and metabolites reinforce barrier function and immune tolerance <cite id="690189ba-1">A hallmark trait of many skin diseases is an aberrant microbiome accompanying a breakdown in skin barrier function and increased risk of infection… occupation of skin niches provides protection by competitive exclusion and antimicrobial molecules</cite><cite id="690189ba-4">In SSc, decreased lipophilic taxa and increased gram-negative taxa accompany increased inflammatory gene signatures</cite>. In psoriasis, reduced microbial diversity and decreased Actinobacteria/Cutibacterium with increased Corynebacterium and Streptococcus align with inflammation severity, and restoration of commensal dominance is linked to improved immune homeostasis, while expansion of non-commensal species promotes inflammation and barrier impairment <cite id="690189ba-2">Psoriatic skin shows decreased microbial diversity and lower Actinobacteria with increased Corynebacterium associated with inflammation severity; increased Streptococcus; Staphylococcus epidermidis more common in normal skin; decrease of commensals and increase of non-commensals alter homeostasis and barrier functions</cite>. In acne, lipid-rich follicles select for Cutibacterium that induce IL-17/IFN-γ responses, with vitamin A and D counteracting Th17 differentiation; this illustrates host-microbe metabolic and immune coupling in which sebaceous lipids fuel pathogen fitness and immune activation, whereas targeted modulation can rebalance inflammation <cite id="a44049b3-0">Cutibacterium acnes induces IL-17A and IFN-γ and promotes Th17/Th1 responses; increased serum IL-17 in acne scarring</cite><cite id="a44049b3-3">Vitamin A and D inhibit P. acnes–induced Th17 differentiation</cite>. Collectively, these mechanisms explain why barrier repair, antimicrobial stewardship that preserves commensals, and immune modulation often synergize in treatment paradigms across inflammatory skin diseases <cite id="690189ba-1">Modulation of the cutaneous inflammatory response, promotion of epidermal differentiation, and enhancement of wound healing are critical processes that the skin microbiota has been implicated in</cite><cite id="f14b695c-0">T cells induced by Staphylococcus epidermidis have been demonstrated to accelerate wound healing in mice</cite>.

# Practical implications and open questions

Commensal skin bacteria like S. epidermidis and Cutibacterium provide direct antimicrobial products (LTA, bacteriocins, phenol-soluble modulins) and indirectly bolster defenses by inducing AMPs, γδ T-cell activity, and regulatory T-cell tolerance; maintaining their abundance is protective, while indiscriminate antibiotics risk selecting for pathogens like S. aureus and gram-negatives with inflammatory signatures <cite id="f14b695c-0">S. epidermidis activates γδ T cells and induces perforin-2; LTA from S. epidermidis mitigates inflammation via TLR2</cite><cite id="f14b695c-1">S. epidermidis produces diverse bacteriocins, including epidermicin</cite><cite id="f14b695c-4">S. epidermidis bacteriocins and PSMs synergize with TLR2-mediated AMPs to control S. aureus and S. pyogenes</cite><cite id="690189ba-4">Skin dysbiosis with decreased lipophilic taxa and increased gram-negatives associates with increased inflammatory signatures</cite>. Conversely, colonization by S. aureus increases inflammatory cytokines and disrupts barrier function via virulence factors, while commensals counteract colonization through niche exclusion and biofilm disruption—principles exploited in atopic dermatitis management and in the development of microbiome-informed therapeutics <cite id="f14b695c-2">Colonization by Staphylococcus aureus increases inflammatory responses within the skin</cite><cite id="f14b695c-3">S. epidermidis inhibits S. aureus biofilm formation and secretion of bacteriocins/PSMs contributes to control</cite>. Key open questions include how to precisely manipulate community composition to favor commensals in chronic disease, how to harness lipid-dependent antagonists (e.g., C16:1 fatty acids) therapeutically, and how to define pediatric windows of immune education for different taxa <cite id="f14b695c-0">Neonatal colonization by S. epidermidis vs. S. aureus imprints distinct T-cell fates, highlighting a critical early-life window</cite><cite id="f14b695c-3">Sapienic and palmitoleic acids exhibit selective antibacterial activity against S. aureus and are lower in atopic dermatitis, suggesting lipid-targeted approaches</cite>.

In sum, the skin microbiome is a habitat-specific community where commensals—dominant in healthy skin—anchor barrier and immune homeostasis via direct antimicrobial metabolites, PRR/TLR signaling, γδ T and regulatory T-cell education, and competitive exclusion, while pathogenic or dysbiotic taxa—often enriched after barrier loss—bias immunity toward Th1/Th17/neutrophilic inflammation that disrupts the epidermis and promotes disease; restoring commensal dominance and repairing the barrier are central to rebalancing immune tone across conditions such as atopic dermatitis, acne, psoriasis, and scleroderma <cite id="690189ba-1">The skin microbiome actively maintains barrier function and modulates inflammation and wound healing; commensals protect via competitive exclusion and antimicrobial molecules, with context-dependent roles</cite><cite id="f14b695c-0">S. epidermidis colonization promotes Treg tolerance and wound-healing T cells, whereas S. aureus promotes IL-1β and Th17 bias</cite><cite id="a44049b3-0">Cutibacterium acnes drives mixed Th1/Th17 responses and elevated IL-17 in acne</cite><cite id="f14b695c-3">S. aureus toxins and proteases disrupt epidermal barrier, while S. epidermidis bacteriocins/PSMs and AMPs counter S. aureus colonization</cite><cite id="690189ba-2">Disease-associated shifts (psoriasis) include reduced Cutibacterium and increased Corynebacterium/Streptococcus with impaired homeostasis</cite><cite id="690189ba-4">Dysbiosis with decreased lipophilic taxa and increased gram-negatives links to heightened inflammatory signatures</cite>.

Title: Living in Your Skin: Microbes, Molecules, and Mechanisms
Snippet: Although the skin functions to keep harmful microbes out, it is also estimated to provide nearly 30 m 2 of diverse microbial habitat (10). Across the moist, sebaceous, or dry microenvironments of the skin are distinct microbial communities encompassing bacteria, fungi, viruses, and microeukaryotes. In this review, members of these communities are referred to as skin commensals, which we define as microorganisms whose interactions on the skin are either neutral or beneficial. Collectively, the skin microbiota have been implicated in the healthy development of an intact barrier throughout the life span. For example, cooperation between commensal microbes and hair follicles during a defined window of development in early life is required for skin immune cell homeostasis and mediating tolerance to commensal bacteria (11,12). In aging individuals, physiological changes to the skin are concomitant with changes to the microbiome and a loss of phylogenetic diversity (13) (Fig. 1). That the skin represents a changing ecosystem intimately tied to its microbiome means that skin microbiome signatures are the most accurate predictor of chronological age, superior to oral or gut microbiome signatures (13)(14)(15)(16). Members of the skin microbiome are not merely hitchhikers either, but active participants helping to maintain the integrity of the skin barrier. Modulation of the cutaneous inflammatory response, promotion of epidermal differentiation, and enhancement of wound healing are only a few examples of critical barrier function processes that the skin microbiota have been implicated in (11,12,17,18). 

A hallmark trait of many skin diseases is an aberrant microbiome accompanying a breakdown in skin barrier function and increased risk of infection. Occupation of skin niches by the microbiome provides protection against invading pathogens by both direct and indirect mechanisms, such as by competitive exclusion (indirect) and by the biosynthesis of microbiome-derived antimicrobial molecules (direct) (19,20). However, the role of commensals residing on the skin is context dependent, with some species pivoting between healthy and diseased states.
</snippet>

Title: The Use of Microbial Modifying Therapies to Prevent Psoriasis Exacerbation and Associated Cardiovascular Comorbidity
Snippet: Skin, the largest organ of the body that provides a physical barrier to injury and microbial insults, harbors abundant and diverse collection of millions of bacteria, fungi, and viruses. Skin microbiome bacteria are mostly from Firmicutes, Actinobacteria, Bacteroidetes, and Proteobacteria phyla [50]. Due to variations in temperature, moisture, and pH value of the skin at different body regions, each site provides a unique colonization environment and, therefore, favors the survival of some bacteria over others. 

The commensal bacteria present in the skin under normal conditions favor the maintenance the immunological homeostasis through mechanisms that include induction of tolerogenic dendritic cells in early life and priming of regulatory T cells protecting from immune responses towards commensal-derived antigens. Emerging evidence indicates that skin dendritic cells can present antigens from skin microbiota and that this mechanism, in neonatal life, is essential to correctly develop tolerance to commensals [51,52]. For this reason, a decrease of commensal bacteria and the increase of non-commensal species could alter the skin immune homeostasis, favoring the generation of inflammatory responses and leading to impaired barrier functions [53]. 

Analysis of the skin microbiome in psoriatic plaques and normal skin of patients with psoriasis as well as in the skin of healthy subjects indicated, as a major variation, a decrease in microbial diversity in psoriatic plaques. Specifically, there was a variation in the relative abundance of Firmicutes, Actinobacteria, and Proteobacteria with a prevalence of Firmicutes in psoriatic skin lesions and a significantly lower level of Actinobacteria compared to healthy and non-lesional skin. Other studies report a decreased representation of Cutibacterium, Burkholderia spp., and Lactobacilli in psoriatic skin. By contrast, the abundance of Corynebacterium was increased in lesional skin and associated with the severity of inflammation [54,55]. An increased abundance of Streptococcus spp. in psoriatic skin has also been reported whereas Staphylococcus epidermidis was more common in normal skin [53,56].
</snippet>

Title: Systemic Sclerosis and Microbiota: Overview of Current Research Trends and Future Perspective
Snippet: The commensal microbiota colonizing the skin surface is essential to skin physiology and immunity [89]. Disruptions in skin microbial communities may contribute to triggering skin autoimmune diseases [90]. Skin resident microbes play an important role in skin health through interactions with other microbes, host epithelium, and the immune system. Commensal microbes produce bioactive metabolites that kill pathogens and stimulate keratinocytes and immune cells to modulate innate and adaptive immune responses, protecting our body against toxic and foreign substances. Keratinocytes sample the microbiota through PRRs that recognize PAMPs such as flagellin and LPS from gram-negative bacteria, and peptidoglycan and lipoteichoic acid (LTA) from gram-positive bacteria [91]. In turn, this process induces the secretion of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) and immune mediators by keratinocytes, and the activation of epidermal and dermal immune cells. Indeed, Staphylococcus epidermidis, a skin commensal, triggers AMP expression by keratinocytes, and LTA produced by S. epidermidis mitigates the cutaneous inflammation through TLR2 signaling [92]. These findings show that the skin microflora can modulate cutaneous immune responses. 

Thus, skin specimens can provide direct information about the microbial community and the immune system in SSc. # Overview: What the skin microbiome is and why “commensal vs pathogen” is a spectrum

The skin hosts diverse microbial communities that occupy moist, sebaceous, and dry microenvironments and include bacteria, fungi, viruses, and microeukaryotes; by definition, “commensals” are microbes with neutral or beneficial interactions with the host, while “pathogens” cause disease, though many taxa straddle a continuum depending on context and host state <cite id="690189ba-1">Across the moist, sebaceous, or dry microenvironments of the skin are distinct microbial communities encompassing bacteria, fungi, viruses, and microeukaryotes… members are referred to as skin commensals, which we define as microorganisms whose interactions on the skin are either neutral or beneficial</cite>. Skin colonization is shaped by site-specific pH, moisture, salinity, and sebum, as well as genotype, age, and sex, with early studies already listing Staphylococcus, Propionibacterium (now Cutibacterium), Micrococcus, and Corynebacterium among abundant genera <cite id="690189ba-0">Abundant bacterial genera on the surface layers of the human skin include Staphylococcus, Propionibacterium, Micrococcus, and Corynebacterium… composition varies with body site (pH, moisture, salinity, sebum) and factors such as genotype, age, and sex</cite>. The skin microbiome is an active participant in barrier integrity, modulating inflammation, promoting epidermal differentiation, and enhancing wound healing, while also protecting against invaders via competitive exclusion and direct antimicrobial metabolites; yet its role is context dependent, shifting between health and disease with ecological change <cite id="690189ba-1">Members of the skin microbiome are not merely hitchhikers… modulate the cutaneous inflammatory response, promotion of epidermal differentiation, and enhancement of wound healing… occupation of skin niches provides protection by competitive exclusion and microbiome-derived antimicrobial molecules; the role of commensals is context dependent</cite>.

Habitat dictates taxa: lipid-rich sebaceous areas favor Propionibacterium/Cutibacterium and Staphylococcus, whereas drier sites harbor more Corynebacterium and Bacilli; phyla commonly include Firmicutes and Actinobacteria, with regional shifts across body sites <cite id="690189ba-0">Abundant bacterial genera… include Staphylococcus, Propionibacterium, Micrococcus, and Corynebacterium</cite><cite id="690189ba-2">Skin microbiome bacteria are mostly from Firmicutes, Actinobacteria, Bacteroidetes, and Proteobacteria… variation in temperature, moisture, and pH favors survival of some bacteria over others</cite>. Commensal microbes educate and calibrate skin immunity. The recent surveys have a greatly advanced understanding of the host-symbiont and host-pathogen relationships and established that the skin microbiota plays a beneficial role, much like the gut microbiota, indicating that the bacteria present on our skin have similar functions in immune regulation and disease pathogenesis [11,13,14]. 

Commensal bacteria can passively occupy a similar ecological niche to a pathogenic microbe, thus impeding its skin colonization. Additionally, commensal bacteria on human skin can selectively induce antimicrobial peptides production and provide a protective effect in vivo when administered before the infectious challenge. The human microbiome may also modulate the immune system, directing it to eliminate the disease-causing factor [14,15].

Title: Living in Your Skin: Microbes, Molecules, and Mechanisms
Snippet: Although the skin functions to keep harmful microbes out, it is also estimated to provide nearly 30 m 2 of diverse microbial habitat (10). Across the moist, sebaceous, or dry microenvironments of the skin are distinct microbial communities encompassing bacteria, fungi, viruses, and microeukaryotes. In this review, members of these communities are referred to as skin commensals, which we define as microorganisms whose interactions on the skin are either neutral or beneficial. Collectively, the skin microbiota have been implicated in the healthy development of an intact barrier throughout the life span. For example, cooperation between commensal microbes and hair follicles during a defined window of development in early life is required for skin immune cell homeostasis and mediating tolerance to commensal bacteria (11,12). In aging individuals, physiological changes to the skin are concomitant with changes to the microbiome and a loss of phylogenetic diversity (13) (Fig. 1). That the skin represents a changing ecosystem intimately tied to its microbiome means that skin microbiome signatures are the most accurate predictor of chronological age, superior to oral or gut microbiome signatures (13)(14)(15)(16). Members of the skin microbiome are not merely hitchhikers either, but active participants helping to maintain the integrity of the skin barrier. Modulation of the cutaneous inflammatory response, promotion of epidermal differentiation, and enhancement of wound healing are only a few examples of critical barrier function processes that the skin microbiota have been implicated in (11,12,17,18). 

A hallmark trait of many skin diseases is an aberrant microbiome accompanying a breakdown in skin barrier function and increased risk of infection. Occupation of skin niches by the microbiome provides protection against invading pathogens by both direct and indirect mechanisms, such as by competitive exclusion (indirect) and by the biosynthesis of microbiome-derived antimicrobial molecules (direct) (19,20). However, the role of commensals residing on the skin is context dependent, with some species pivoting between healthy and diseased states.

Title: The Use of Microbial Modifying Therapies to Prevent Psoriasis Exacerbation and Associated Cardiovascular Comorbidity
Snippet: Skin, the largest organ of the body that provides a physical barrier to injury and microbial insults, harbors abundant and diverse collection of millions of bacteria, fungi, and viruses. Skin microbiome bacteria are mostly from Firmicutes, Actinobacteria, Bacteroidetes, and Proteobacteria phyla [50]. Due to variations in temperature, moisture, and pH value of the skin at different body regions, each site provides a unique colonization environment and, therefore, favors the survival of some bacteria over others. 

The commensal bacteria present in the skin under normal conditions favor the maintenance the immunological homeostasis through mechanisms that include induction of tolerogenic dendritic cells in early life and priming of regulatory T cells protecting from immune responses towards commensal-derived antigens. Emerging evidence indicates that skin dendritic cells can present antigens from skin microbiota and that this mechanism, in neonatal life, is essential to correctly develop tolerance to commensals [51,52]. For this reason, a decrease of commensal bacteria and the increase of non-commensal species could alter the skin immune homeostasis, favoring the generation of inflammatory responses and leading to impaired barrier functions [53]. 

Analysis of the skin microbiome in psoriatic plaques and normal skin of patients with psoriasis as well as in the skin of healthy subjects indicated, as a major variation, a decrease in microbial diversity in psoriatic plaques. Specifically, there was a variation in the relative abundance of Firmicutes, Actinobacteria, and Proteobacteria with a prevalence of Firmicutes in psoriatic skin lesions and a significantly lower level of Actinobacteria compared to healthy and non-lesional skin. Other studies report a decreased representation of Cutibacterium, Burkholderia spp., and Lactobacilli in psoriatic skin. By contrast, the abundance of Corynebacterium was increased in lesional skin and associated with the severity of inflammation [54,55]. An increased abundance of Streptococcus spp. in psoriatic skin has also been reported whereas Staphylococcus epidermidis was more common in normal skin [53,56].

Title: Systemic Sclerosis and Microbiota: Overview of Current Research Trends and Future Perspective
Snippet: The commensal microbiota colonizing the skin surface is essential to skin physiology and immunity [89]. Disruptions in skin microbial communities may contribute to triggering skin autoimmune diseases [90]. Skin resident microbes play an important role in skin health through interactions with other microbes, host epithelium, and the immune system. Commensal microbes produce bioactive metabolites that kill pathogens and stimulate keratinocytes and immune cells to modulate innate and adaptive immune responses, protecting our body against toxic and foreign substances. Keratinocytes sample the microbiota through PRRs that recognize PAMPs such as flagellin and LPS from gram-negative bacteria, and peptidoglycan and lipoteichoic acid (LTA) from gram-positive bacteria [91]. In turn, this process induces the secretion of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) and immune mediators by keratinocytes, and the activation of epidermal and dermal immune cells. Indeed, Staphylococcus epidermidis, a skin commensal, triggers AMP expression by keratinocytes, and LTA produced by S. epidermidis mitigates the cutaneous inflammation through TLR2 signaling [92]. These findings show that the skin microflora can modulate cutaneous immune responses. 

Thus, skin specimens can provide direct information about the microbial community and the immune system in SSc. In studies using skin samples from SSc patients, no significant differences in the bacterial microbiome were found, except for the increased expression of Rhodotorula glutinis [93]. Moreover, Johnson et al. [59] discovered substantial changes in the skin microbial composition, with decreased lipophilic taxa (Propionibacterium) and increased gram-negative taxa (Burkholderia, Citrobacter, and Vibrio). Skin microbial dysbiosis is associated with an increased inflammatory gene signature, which might help to explore components of the immune system that are relevant to SSc pathogenesis [84]. Nevertheless, there are no data on immune-skin microbe interactions and its mechanisms in SSc.

Title: Meta Analysis of Skin Microbiome: New Link between Skin Microbiota Diversity and Skin Health with Proposal to Use This as a Future Mechanism to Determine Whether Cosmetic Products Damage the Skin
Snippet: The intestinal microflora and its links to immune system function and overall health has been the subject of much research and discussion in recent years [1,2]. The idea that commensal microbes in the gut need to be encouraged, not destroyed [3], has led to the topic becoming mainstream and inspiring high street books such as "Let Them Eat Dirt" [4]. There is now a prevailing belief in a causal link between ill-health and unbalanced gut flora [5], and the probability that it is western lifestyles that are affecting the composition and diversity of the gut microbiota leading to many chronic health problems [6]. Yet despite the rapid rise in allergy related skin-health problems in the developed world [7], parallel research into the role of the skin microbiome and the body's immune system responses on overall health has been very limited. 

The skin is the largest organ [8,9] and is host to an enormously diverse array of microbes [10]. Only now is the crucial role that the skin plays in overall health starting to be understood; most early literature on skin microbiota concentrates on the pathogenic roles of different types of microbiota on the skin, yet little research has been done on the influence of resident cutaneous microflora on skin health [11]. The bacterial colonies inhabiting the skin have been found to be crucial for defence of the host [12,13], and are suggested to only rarely become pathogenic, being commensal (harmless and very rarely associated with disease) or symbiotic (good) the majority of the time. They live in peaceful co-existence with the host, sheltered in the specific ecological environment [11,[14][15][16][17]. The relationship has been described as "mutualistically symbiotic" instead of commensally symbiotic, as both parties benefit [15,18,19]. 

Microbes make up part of the skin barrier, which, together with a person's innate immunity, combine to form a delicate balance needed to maintain healthy skin. If this balance is disturbed, the host becomes more susceptible to inflammatory diseases and cutaneous infections [11,20,21].

Members of the skin microbiome are not merely hitchhikers either, but active participants helping to maintain the integrity of the skin barrier. Modulation of the cutaneous inflammatory response, promotion of epidermal differentiation, and enhancement of wound healing are only a few examples of critical barrier function processes that the skin microbiota have been implicated in (11,12,17,18). 

A hallmark trait of many skin diseases is an aberrant microbiome accompanying a breakdown in skin barrier function and increased risk of infection. Occupation of skin niches by the microbiome provides protection against invading pathogens by both direct and indirect mechanisms, such as by competitive exclusion (indirect) and by the biosynthesis of microbiome-derived antimicrobial molecules (direct) (19,20). However, the role of commensals residing on the skin is context dependent, with some species pivoting between healthy and diseased states.

Skin, the largest organ of the body that provides a physical barrier to injury and microbial insults, harbors abundant and diverse collection of millions of bacteria, fungi, and viruses. Skin microbiome bacteria are mostly from Firmicutes, Actinobacteria, Bacteroidetes, and Proteobacteria phyla [50]. Due to variations in temperature, moisture, and pH value of the skin at different body regions, each site provides a unique colonization environment and, therefore, favors the survival of some bacteria over others. 

The commensal bacteria present in the skin under normal conditions favor the maintenance the immunological homeostasis through mechanisms that include induction of tolerogenic dendritic cells in early life and priming of regulatory T cells protecting from immune responses towards commensal-derived antigens. Emerging evidence indicates that skin dendritic cells can present antigens from skin microbiota and that this mechanism, in neonatal life, is essential to correctly develop tolerance to commensals [51,52]. For this reason, a decrease of commensal bacteria and the increase of non-commensal species could alter the skin immune homeostasis, favoring the generation of inflammatory responses and leading to impaired barrier functions [53]. 

Analysis of the skin microbiome in psoriatic plaques and normal skin of patients with psoriasis as well as in the skin of healthy subjects indicated, as a major variation, a decrease in microbial diversity in psoriatic plaques. Specifically, there was a variation in the relative abundance of Firmicutes, Actinobacteria, and Proteobacteria with a prevalence of Firmicutes in psoriatic skin lesions and a significantly lower level of Actinobacteria compared to healthy and non-lesional skin. Other studies report a decreased representation of Cutibacterium, Burkholderia spp., and Lactobacilli in psoriatic skin. By contrast, the abundance of Corynebacterium was increased in lesional skin and associated with the severity of inflammation [54,55]. An increased abundance of Streptococcus spp. in psoriatic skin has also been reported whereas Staphylococcus epidermidis was more common in normal skin [53,56].

The commensal microbiota colonizing the skin surface is essential to skin physiology and immunity [89]. Disruptions in skin microbial communities may contribute to triggering skin autoimmune diseases [90]. Skin resident microbes play an important role in skin health through interactions with other microbes, host epithelium, and the immune system. Commensal microbes produce bioactive metabolites that kill pathogens and stimulate keratinocytes and immune cells to modulate innate and adaptive immune responses, protecting our body against toxic and foreign substances. Keratinocytes sample the microbiota through PRRs that recognize PAMPs such as flagellin and LPS from gram-negative bacteria, and peptidoglycan and lipoteichoic acid (LTA) from gram-positive bacteria [91]. In turn, this process induces the secretion of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) and immune mediators by keratinocytes, and the activation of epidermal and dermal immune cells. Indeed, Staphylococcus epidermidis, a skin commensal, triggers AMP expression by keratinocytes, and LTA produced by S. epidermidis mitigates the cutaneous inflammation through TLR2 signaling [92]. These findings show that the skin microflora can modulate cutaneous immune responses. 

Thus, skin specimens can provide direct information about the microbial community and the immune system in SSc. In studies using skin samples from SSc patients, no significant differences in the bacterial microbiome were found, except for the increased expression of Rhodotorula glutinis [93]. Moreover, Johnson et al. [59] discovered substantial changes in the skin microbial composition, with decreased lipophilic taxa (Propionibacterium) and increased gram-negative taxa (Burkholderia, Citrobacter, and Vibrio). Skin microbial dysbiosis is associated with an increased inflammatory gene signature, which might help to explore components of the immune system that are relevant to SSc pathogenesis [84]. Nevertheless, there are no data on immune-skin microbe interactions and its mechanisms in SSc.

The intestinal microflora and its links to immune system function and overall health has been the subject of much research and discussion in recent years [1,2]. The idea that commensal microbes in the gut need to be encouraged, not destroyed [3], has led to the topic becoming mainstream and inspiring high street books such as "Let Them Eat Dirt" [4]. There is now a prevailing belief in a causal link between ill-health and unbalanced gut flora [5], and the probability that it is western lifestyles that are affecting the composition and diversity of the gut microbiota leading to many chronic health problems [6]. Yet despite the rapid rise in allergy related skin-health problems in the developed world [7], parallel research into the role of the skin microbiome and the body's immune system responses on overall health has been very limited. 

The skin is the largest organ [8,9] and is host to an enormously diverse array of microbes [10]. Only now is the crucial role that the skin plays in overall health starting to be understood; most early literature on skin microbiota concentrates on the pathogenic roles of different types of microbiota on the skin, yet little research has been done on the influence of resident cutaneous microflora on skin health [11]. The bacterial colonies inhabiting the skin have been found to be crucial for defence of the host [12,13], and are suggested to only rarely become pathogenic, being commensal (harmless and very rarely associated with disease) or symbiotic (good) the majority of the time. They live in peaceful co-existence with the host, sheltered in the specific ecological environment [11,[14][15][16][17]. The relationship has been described as "mutualistically symbiotic" instead of commensally symbiotic, as both parties benefit [15,18,19]. 

Microbes make up part of the skin barrier, which, together with a person's innate immunity, combine to form a delicate balance needed to maintain healthy skin. If this balance is disturbed, the host becomes more susceptible to inflammatory diseases and cutaneous infections [11,20,21].

Title: Interactions between Host Immunity and Skin-Colonizing Staphylococci: No Two Siblings Are Alike
Snippet: As the outermost layer of the body, the skin harbors innumerable and varied microorganisms. These microorganisms interact with the host, and these interactions contribute to host immunity. One of the most abundant genera of skin commensals is Staphylococcus. Bacteria belonging to this genus are some of the most influential commensals that reside on the skin. For example, colonization by Staphylococcus aureus, a well-known pathogen, increases inflammatory responses within the skin. Conversely, colonization by Staphylococcus epidermis, a coagulase-negative staphylococcal species that are prevalent throughout the skin, can be innocuous or beneficial. Thus, manipulating the abundance of these two bacterial species likely alters the skin microbiome and modulates the cutaneous immune response, with potential implications for various inflammation-associated skin diseases. Importantly, before researchers can begin manipulating the skin microbiome to prevent and treat disease, they must first fully understand how these two species can modulate the cutaneous immune response. In this review, we discuss the nature of the interactions between these two bacterial species and immune cells within the skin, discussing their immunogenicity within the context of skin disorders.

Title: A narrative review of research progress on the role of NLRP3 inflammasome in acne vulgaris
Snippet: In addition to Th1 and Th2 cells, Th17 cells can complement the function of CD4 + T cells family lineages (14). During inflammatory processes, CD4 + T cells play an essential role in balancing adaptive immunity. Cutibacterium acnes can promote mixed Th17/Th1 responses by inducing CD4 + T cells secreting IL-17A and interferon-gamma (IFN-γ). IL-17 and IL-22, the main Th17 effector cytokines, promote antimicrobial responses by inducing a series of AMPs (55,56). Sebocytes stimulated by Cutibacterium acnes promote the activation of Th17 cell types via the secretion of IL-6, IL-1β, and growth factor-β (57). A recent study showed that CD4 + Th17 clones with the same antibacterial properties as cytotoxic T cells and granulocytes killed bacteria in the IL-26-independent pathway (14). These CD4 + Th17 clones were produced by monocyte culture of acne strains in healthy skin, which was not related to acne. These findings suggest that the antibacterial mechanism of the Th17 subgroup involves a unique relationship between innate immunity and adaptive immunity (14). Proinflammatory IL-17-generating cells and anti-inflammatory FOXP3 + Treg cells are the main factors for CD4 + T cells to play a crucial role in inflammatory diseases. In acne vulgaris, the expression levels of IL-17 and FOXP3 are increased in epidermal keratinocytes and lymphocytes (58). Cutibacterium acnes can induce the activation of IL-17, with one study finding that the expression of serum IL-17 was increased in patients with acne vulgaris scarring compared to those without (59). 

Further research proves that IL-17 expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells is significantly increased in the skin of acne vulgaris patients with Cutibacterium acnes strains compared to healthy skin with Cutibacterium acnes strains (55,57).

Title: Propionibacterium acnes induces an interleukin-17 response in acne vulgaris that is regulated by vitamin A and vitamin D
Snippet: Acne vulgaris is the most common skin disorder affecting millions of people worldwide and inflammation resulting from the immune response targeting Propionibacterium acnes plays a significant role in its pathogenesis. In this study, we have demonstrated that P. acnes is a potent inducer of Th17 and Th1, but not Th2 responses in human PBMCs. P. acnes stimulated expression of key Th17-related genes, including IL-17A, RORα, RORc, IL-17RA and IL-17RC, and triggered IL-17 secretion from CD4+, but not CD8+ T cells. Supernatants from P. acnes-stimulated PBMCs were sufficient to promote the differentiation of naïve CD4+CD45RA T cells into Th17 cells. Furthermore, we found that the combination of IL-1β, IL-6 and TGF-β neutralizing antibodies completely inhibited P. acnes-induced IL-17 production. Importantly, we showed that IL-17-expressing cells were present in skin biopsies from acne patients but not from normal donors. Finally, vitamin A (all-trans retinoic acid) and vitamin D (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3) inhibited P. acnes-induced Th17 differentiation. Together, our data demonstrate that IL-17 is induced by P. acnes and expressed in acne lesions and that both vitamin A and vitamin D could be effective tools to modulate Th17-mediated diseases such as acne.

Snippet: The IL-17 levels are elevated in acne lesions. IL-6, IL-23, and TGF-b are highly expressed in addition to IL-17A, IL-22, IL-26, TNF-a as well as the chemokines CSF2 and CCL20. snippet.text: Acne vulgaris is the most common skin disorder affecting millions of people worldwide and inflammation resulting from the immune response targeting Propionibacterium acnes plays a significant role in its pathogenesis. In this study, we have demonstrated that P. acnes is a potent inducer of Th17 and Th1, but not Th2 responses in human PBMCs. P. acnes stimulated expression of key Th17-related genes, including IL-17A, RORα, RORc, IL-17RA and IL-17RC, and triggered IL-17 secretion from CD4+, but not CD8+ T cells. Supernatants from P. acnes-stimulated PBMCs were sufficient to promote the differentiation of naïve CD4+CD45RA T cells into Th17 cells. Furthermore, we found that the combination of IL-1β, IL-6 and TGF-β neutralizing antibodies completely inhibited P. acnes-induced IL-17 production. Importantly, we showed that IL-17-expressing cells were present in skin biopsies from acne patients but not from normal donors. Finally, vitamin A (all-trans retinoic acid) and vitamin D (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3) inhibited P. acnes-induced Th17 differentiation. Together, our data demonstrate that IL-17 is induced by P. acnes and expressed in acne lesions and that both vitamin A and vitamin D could be effective tools to modulate Th17-mediated diseases such as acne.

The combined expression of CXCR3 and CD161 was present in 15% of conventional T cells, reminiscent of pathogenic Th17.1 lymphocytes (43). # Overview: Composition and Ecology of the Skin Microbiome

Across skin microenvironments (dry, moist, sebaceous), the dominant bacteria include Staphylococcus, Propionibacterium/Cutibacterium, Corynebacterium, and Micrococcus, with composition shaped by site-specific factors such as pH, moisture, sebum, age, sex, and genotype, and by environmental exposures <cite id="e1c817a5-0">Abundant bacterial genera on human skin include Staphylococcus, Propionibacterium, Micrococcus, and Corynebacterium, and composition varies by body site and factors including pH, moisture, salinity, sebum, genotype, age, and sex</cite>. The skin microbiome is a dynamic ecosystem whose shifts accompany barrier disruption and disease, and whose members provide direct antimicrobial products and indirect colonization resistance to keep pathogens at bay <cite id="e1c817a5-1">Members of the skin microbiota are active participants that maintain barrier integrity, modulate inflammation, promote epidermal differentiation, and enhance wound healing; occupation of niches provides protection by competitive exclusion and microbiome-derived antimicrobials</cite>. Commensals are typically defined as microbes whose interactions are neutral or beneficial; they are essential for immune development and barrier homeostasis, with context-dependent roles that can pivot during disease <cite id="e1c817a5-1">Commensals are microorganisms whose interactions on the skin are neutral or beneficial, cooperate with follicles in early life to establish immune homeostasis and tolerance, and their roles are context dependent, sometimes shifting between healthy and diseased states</cite>.

# Commensals versus Pathogens: What Distinguishes the Two Groups?

Commensal skin bacteria tend to occupy niches that limit colonization by pathogens via competitive exclusion, produce or induce antimicrobial peptides and fatty-acid–derived acids that lower pH, and program tolerogenic or repair-skewed immune responses, especially when exposure occurs in early life <cite id="e1c817a5-0">Commensal bacteria can passively occupy niches similar to pathogens to impede colonization, and selectively induce antimicrobial peptides that provide protection in vivo; the microbiome directs the immune system to eliminate disease-causing factors</cite><cite id="e1c817a5-1">Occupation of skin niches provides protection by competitive exclusion and by biosynthesis of microbiome-derived antimicrobial molecules, and cooperation with follicles in early life is required for immune homeostasis and tolerance</cite>. For example, Cutibacterium acnes is a common sebaceous follicle commensal that metabolizes sebum-derived fatty acids, lowers surface pH, and inhibits pathogenic staphylococci, thereby promoting barrier homeostasis; multiple subtypes with differing pathogenic potential coexist on skin, and genotype correlates with acne involvement <cite id="095524f8-0">Cutibacterium acnes is a common commensal in sebaceous follicles that metabolizes free fatty acids from sebum, reducing surface pH and inhibiting Staphylococcus aureus while promoting other commensals; C. acnes has subtypes (type I–III) with differing associations with acne</cite>. By contrast, pathogenic or dysbiotic taxa (e.g., S. aureus overgrowth in atopic dermatitis; lipase- and hyaluronidase-expressing Cutibacterium phylotypes in acne; reduced diversity with pathogen dominance in psoriasis) exploit barrier defects to trigger inflammation and infection, often via virulence mechanisms such as biofilm formation, proteases, lipases, and immunogenic proteins that activate complement and innate sensors <cite id="095524f8-1">In acne, lipophilic Cutibacterium acnes proliferates in the pilosebaceous unit, secretes hyaluronases and lipases that damage the unit, encodes immunogenic proteins activating complement, and biofilms and type 1A1 phylogroups are associated with disease; in atopic dermatitis, Staphylococcus aureus increases during flares while diversity decreases</cite><cite id="095524f8-2">Psoriatic skin shows decreased normal commensals (Staphylococcus epidermidis, Propionibacterium acnes) and increased opportunistic Staphylococcus aureus, consistent with dysbiosis-driven susceptibility</cite><cite id="095524f8-3">In atopic dermatitis, reduced microbial diversity with Staphylococcus aureus overgrowth and decreased commensals (Streptococcus, Corynebacterium, Cutibacterium) is common; in psoriasis, Corynebacterium, Lactobacillus, and Cutibacterium acnes are decreased</cite><cite id="095524f8-4">Dermatological dysbiosis features pathogenic overgrowth and reduced diversity that drive immune dysregulation; acne and rosacea involve shifts to inflammatory Cutibacterium phylotypes and Demodex with biofilm formation; chronic wounds show pathogen dominance and biofilm persistence</cite>.

Functionally, commensals like Staphylococcus epidermidis often elicit anti-inflammatory, tolerance-promoting programs (e.g., Treg accumulation and IL-1–mediated, but restrained, responses) when exposure occurs early, whereas delayed or pathogen-dominant exposures skew toward effector T cells and inflammation <cite id="8da6d071-0">Neonatal colonization with Staphylococcus epidermidis promotes Treg activation and tolerance, whereas neonatal S. aureus colonization upregulates IL-1β and shifts the Th17:Treg ratio; commensal colonization increases IL-17A/IFN-γ T cells and S100A8/6 while keratinocytes upregulate MHCII and Th1 accumulation</cite><cite id="8da6d071-2">Neonatal exposure to S. epidermidis expands epidermal Tregs and suppresses Th17 responses, while delayed colonization in adults induces CD8+ effector T cells and an inflammatory phenotype</cite>. Mechanistically, S. epidermidis components such as lipoteichoic acid engage TLR2 to drive IL-1β maturation in keratinocytes, induce antimicrobial peptides (e.g., β-defensin-3), and simultaneously induce A20 to restrain NF-κB/IL-1β, illustrating how commensals activate host defenses without triggering uncontrolled inflammation <cite id="8da6d071-4">Staphylococcus epidermidis induces keratinocytes to mature and release IL-1β via TLR2, promotes β-defensin-3 and often synergizes with TGF-α to enhance protection, and concurrently induces A20 to limit NF-κB and IL-1β, maintaining homeostasis; the IL-1β response to S. epidermidis is subdued compared to pathogenic S. aureus, enabling microbial differentiation and tolerance</cite>. In contrast, pathogenic bacteria can provoke stronger, unregulated innate signaling and adaptive responses via superantigens, proteases, and biofilms, tipping the balance toward Th1/Th17-driven inflammation and barrier compromise <cite id="095524f8-1">Pathogenic or dysbiotic microbes activate classical/alternative complement, induce biofilms, and express proteases (hyaluronases, lipases) that damage tissue and promote inflammation in acne</cite><cite id="095524f8-4">Biofilm persistence and pathogenic dominance drive chronic inflammation and impaired healing in cutaneous disorders</cite>.

# How Commensals Shape Immune Responses

Commensals educate the skin immune system from early life to maintain tolerance and effective defense. Neonatal exposure to S. epidermidis enriches regulatory T cells in the epidermis, supports immune tolerance, and primes rapid repair, whereas exposure to S. aureus skews toward IL-1β elevation and Th17 expansion, demonstrating strain- and timing-dependent immune imprinting <cite id="8da6d071-0">Early-life Staphylococcus epidermidis colonization promotes Treg activation and tolerance, while neonatal Staphylococcus aureus colonization increases IL-1β and shifts toward a higher Th17:Treg ratio</cite><cite id="8da6d071-2">Neonatal S. epidermidis expands Tregs and suppresses Th17 responses in the skin, whereas adult-onset colonization induces CD8+ effector T cells and inflammation</cite>. These commensals also activate tissue-resident dendritic cells and CD8+ T cells that enhance antimicrobial defenses and wound re-epithelialization: S. epidermidis induces CD8+ T-cell accumulation via MHCIb presentation of formyl methionine peptides, with induced CD8+ T cells accelerating wound repair and activating perforin-2 to kill intracellular S. aureus in human skin ex vivo <cite id="8da6d071-1">Staphylococcus epidermidis induces accumulation of CD8+ T lymphocytes via dendritic cells presenting N-formyl methionine peptides; induced CD8+ T cells promote improved re-epithelization and accelerate wound repair</cite><cite id="8da6d071-0">T cells induced by S. epidermidis accelerate wound healing in mice and increase perforin-2 expression, enhancing killing of intracellular Staphylococcus aureus in human skin ex vivo</cite>. Commensal stimulation of innate immunity occurs through γδ T cells and antimicrobial effector molecules: S. epidermidis increases γδ T-cell frequency and induces the antimicrobial protein perforin-2 in human skin ex vivo, improving defense against S. aureus intracellularly, and engages keratinocyte TLR2 to mature IL-1β and induce β-defensin-3 while deploying host dampeners like A20 to prevent overdrive <cite id="8da6d071-3">Topical S. epidermidis increases γδ T cells in colonized human skin ex vivo, confirming colonization and immune activation</cite><cite id="8da6d071-4">S. epidermidis boosts innate responses by activating γδ T cells, inducing perforin-2, and stimulating TLR2-driven IL-1β maturation and β-defensin-3 induction in keratinocytes, with concurrent A20 induction to limit NF-κB and maintain homeostasis</cite>.

Beyond single strains, commensal communities modulate the cutaneous inflammatory response and promote epidermal differentiation and wound healing, providing protection against invading pathogens through direct antimicrobial molecules and indirect barrier support, with evidence that commensal-driven immunity can prevent S. aureus invasion in models and that protective organisms are reduced in cutaneous disorders <cite id="e1c817a5-1">The microbiota modulates cutaneous inflammatory response, promotes epidermal differentiation, and enhances wound healing; commensals provide direct antimicrobials and indirect protection via colonization resistance</cite><cite id="095524f8-2">Human commensals produce antimicrobials that prevent S. aureus infection, and patients with cutaneous disorders are deficient in these protective organisms</cite>.

# How Pathogenic Microbiota Drive Immune Activation and Disease

Title: Living in Your Skin: Microbes, Molecules, and Mechanisms
Snippet: Although the skin functions to keep harmful microbes out, it is also estimated to provide nearly 30 m 2 of diverse microbial habitat (10). Across the moist, sebaceous, or dry microenvironments of the skin are distinct microbial communities encompassing bacteria, fungi, viruses, and microeukaryotes. In this review, members of these communities are referred to as skin commensals, which we define as microorganisms whose interactions on the skin are either neutral or beneficial. Collectively, the skin microbiota have been implicated in the healthy development of an intact barrier throughout the life span. For example, cooperation between commensal microbes and hair follicles during a defined window of development in early life is required for skin immune cell homeostasis and mediating tolerance to commensal bacteria (11,12). In aging individuals, physiological changes to the skin are concomitant with changes to the microbiome and a loss of phylogenetic diversity (13) (Fig. 1). That the skin represents a changing ecosystem intimately tied to its microbiome means that skin microbiome signatures are the most accurate predictor of chronological age, superior to oral or gut microbiome signatures (13)(14)(15)(16). Members of the skin microbiome are not merely hitchhikers either, but active participants helping to maintain the integrity of the skin barrier. Modulation of the cutaneous inflammatory response, promotion of epidermal differentiation, and enhancement of wound healing are only a few examples of critical barrier function processes that the skin microbiota have been implicated in (11,12,17,18). 

A hallmark trait of many skin diseases is an aberrant microbiome accompanying a breakdown in skin barrier function and increased risk of infection. Occupation of skin niches by the microbiome provides protection against invading pathogens by both direct and indirect mechanisms, such as by competitive exclusion (indirect) and by the biosynthesis of microbiome-derived antimicrobial molecules (direct) (19,20). However, the role of commensals residing on the skin is context dependent, with some species pivoting between healthy and diseased states.
</snippet>

Title: Role of Cutaneous Microbiome in Dermatology
Snippet: The cutaneous microflora consists of various microorganisms which interact with host epithelial cells and innate and acquired immunity. This microbial milieu and its interaction with host cells prevent the growth of pathogenic organisms and educate host immunity to fight against harmful microorganisms. The microbial composition depends on various intrinsic and extrinsic factors and an imbalance in the cutaneous microflora predisposes the individual to both infectious and non-infectious diseases. In this review, we describe the commensal microbiome and its variation, the current role of the cutaneous microbiome in the pathogenesis of various dermatological diseases, and their therapeutic implications.

Snippet: Human skin serves as a barrier that separates the external and internal environments. It prevents the invasion of harmful substances into the body and blocks the loss of moisture and beneficial substances from the body. Its surface is home to many microorganisms, including bacteria, fungi, and viruses, which form colonies. These microorganisms interact with each other and with their host, creating a stable and complex ecosystem through cross-talk. This skin microbiome changes with factors such as age, gender, temperature, pH, ultraviolet exposure, moisture and humidity, and sebum content 1,2 . In recent years, comprehensive analyses of the skin microbiome have been conducted using next-generation sequencing techniques, specifically the analysis of bacterial 16S rRNA gene. Reports have been emerging about its involvement in inflammatory skin diseases such as acne vulgaris, atopic dermatitis, and psoriasis [3][4][5][6] . 

Among the skin microbiome, the most common commensal bacterial species is Cutibacterium acnes 7,8 . C. acnes is a ubiquitous Gram-positive anaerobic bacterium belonging to the phylum Actinobacteria and is primarily found deep within the sebaceous hair follicles where it comes into contact with keratinocytes 9 . Furthermore, C. acnes is known to metabolize free fatty acids from sebum, which reduces the surface pH. This acidic environment potentially inhibits pathogenic bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus and promotes the growth of other healthy commensal bacteria, suggesting its contribution to barrier homeostasis [10][11][12] .

Title: CURRENT PERSPECTIVES ON THE ROLE OF THE CUTANEOUS MICROBIOME IN CHRONIC INFLAMMATORY SKIN DISEASES
Snippet: Objective: The skin microbiome is a complex ecosystem of bacteria, viruses, fungi, and archaea that interacts with host cells to regulate defense mechanisms, immune responses, colonization resistance, and tissue repair. This review aims to summarize current knowledge on the role of the skin microbiome in the course and treatment of chronic inflammatory dermatoses, including atopic dermatitis, psoriasis, and acne vulgaris. 
Materials and methods: A literature review was performed using PubMed and Google Scholar databases. Keywords included: skin microbiota, skin microbiome, chronic inflammatory dermatoses, atopic dermatitis, psoriasis, acne vulgaris, microbiome transplantation, probiotics, prebiotics, and postbiotics. A total of 36 articles published between 2008 and 2024 were analyzed for relevance. 
Description: Patients with atopic dermatitis show reduced microbial diversity, characterized by Staphylococcus aureus overgrowth and decreased commensal bacteria such as Streptococcus, Corynebacterium, Cutibacterium, and Proteobacteria. In psoriasis, decreased levels of Corynebacterium spp., Lactobacillus spp., and Cutibacterium acnes are common. Acne vulgaris is linked to excessive sebum production, abnormal follicular keratinization, Cutibacterium acnes colonization, and inflammation. 
Strategies to modulate the skin microbiome include microbiome transplantation and bacteriotherapy, which applies selected beneficial strains to disinfected skin. These methods may offer more practical alternatives than full transplantation. Additionally, prebiotic compounds can promote the growth of protective microbes, while probiotics and postbiotics are increasingly studied for their therapeutic effects. 
Conclusions: Chronic inflammatory dermatoses significantly impair quality of life. Evidence suggests that targeting the skin microbiome holds therapeutic potential. Further studies are needed to clarify microbiota–host interactions, consequences of dysbiosis, and the clinical utility of microbiome-based interventions.

# Overview: Composition and Ecology of the Skin Microbiome

Across skin microenvironments (dry, moist, sebaceous), the dominant bacteria include Staphylococcus, Propionibacterium/Cutibacterium, Corynebacterium, and Micrococcus, with composition shaped by site-specific factors such as pH, moisture, sebum, age, sex, and genotype, and by environmental exposures <cite id="e1c817a5-0">Abundant bacterial genera on human skin include Staphylococcus, Propionibacterium, Micrococcus, and Corynebacterium, and composition varies by body site and factors including pH, moisture, salinity, sebum, genotype, age, and sex</cite>. The skin microbiome is a dynamic ecosystem whose shifts accompany barrier disruption and disease, and whose members provide direct antimicrobial products and indirect colonization resistance to keep pathogens at bay <cite id="e1c817a5-1">Members of the skin microbiota are active participants that maintain barrier integrity, modulate inflammation, promote epidermal differentiation, and enhance wound healing; occupation of niches provides protection by competitive exclusion and microbiome-derived antimicrobials</cite>. Commensals are typically defined as microbes whose interactions are neutral or beneficial; they are essential for immune development and barrier homeostasis, with context-dependent roles that can pivot during disease <cite id="e1c817a5-1">Commensals are microorganisms whose interactions on the skin are neutral or beneficial, cooperate with follicles in early life to establish immune homeostasis and tolerance, and their roles are context dependent, sometimes shifting between healthy and diseased states</cite>.

# Commensals versus Pathogens: What Distinguishes the Two Groups?

By contrast, pathogenic or dysbiotic taxa (e.g., S. aureus overgrowth in atopic dermatitis; lipase- and hyaluronidase-expressing Cutibacterium phylotypes in acne; reduced diversity with pathogen dominance in psoriasis) exploit barrier defects to trigger inflammation and infection, often via virulence mechanisms such as biofilm formation, proteases, lipases, and immunogenic proteins that activate complement and innate sensors <cite id="095524f8-1">In acne, lipophilic Cutibacterium acnes proliferates in the pilosebaceous unit, secretes hyaluronases and lipases that damage the unit, encodes immunogenic proteins activating complement, and biofilms and type 1A1 phylogroups are associated with disease; in atopic dermatitis, Staphylococcus aureus increases during flares while diversity decreases</cite><cite id="095524f8-2">Psoriatic skin shows decreased normal commensals (Staphylococcus epidermidis, Propionibacterium acnes) and increased opportunistic Staphylococcus aureus, consistent with dysbiosis-driven susceptibility</cite><cite id="095524f8-3">In atopic dermatitis, reduced microbial diversity with Staphylococcus aureus overgrowth and decreased commensals (Streptococcus, Corynebacterium, Cutibacterium) is common; in psoriasis, Corynebacterium, Lactobacillus, and Cutibacterium acnes are decreased</cite><cite id="095524f8-4">Dermatological dysbiosis features pathogenic overgrowth and reduced diversity that drive immune dysregulation; acne and rosacea involve shifts to inflammatory Cutibacterium phylotypes and Demodex with biofilm formation; chronic wounds show pathogen dominance and biofilm persistence</cite>.

# How Commensals Shape Immune Responses

Commensals educate the skin immune system from early life to maintain tolerance and effective defense. - Acne vulgaris: Sebum-rich follicles favor Cutibacterium colonization; shifts toward inflammatory C. acnes phylotypes, lipases/hyaluronidases, and biofilms drive follicular damage and inflammation, often superimposed on barrier dysfunction and altered immunity <cite id="095524f8-0">C. acnes metabolism reduces pH and inhibits S. aureus, but multiple subtypes with differing pathogenicity exist</cite><cite id="095524f8-1">In acne, lipophilic C. acnes proliferates, secretes hyaluronases and lipases, activates complement, and biofilms/1A1 phylogroups correlate with disease</cite>.

# Practical Distinguishing Features and Therapeutic Axes

- Composition: Healthy skin favors Staphylococcus, Corynebacterium, Cutibacterium, and Lactobacillus; disease states show decreased diversity with S. aureus expansion (AD/psoriasis) or inflammatory C. acnes phylotypes/biofilms (acne) <cite id="e1c817a5-0">Early studies show abundant Staphylococcus, Propionibacterium, Micrococcus, Corynebacterium</cite><cite id="095524f8-3">AD shows S. aureus overgrowth and decreased commensals; psoriasis shows decreased Corynebacterium, Lactobacillus, and C. acnes</cite><cite id="095524f8-1">Acne associates with C. acnes biofilms and type 1A1 phylogroups</cite>.

Title: Living in Your Skin: Microbes, Molecules, and Mechanisms
Snippet: Although the skin functions to keep harmful microbes out, it is also estimated to provide nearly 30 m 2 of diverse microbial habitat (10). Across the moist, sebaceous, or dry microenvironments of the skin are distinct microbial communities encompassing bacteria, fungi, viruses, and microeukaryotes. In this review, members of these communities are referred to as skin commensals, which we define as microorganisms whose interactions on the skin are either neutral or beneficial. Collectively, the skin microbiota have been implicated in the healthy development of an intact barrier throughout the life span. For example, cooperation between commensal microbes and hair follicles during a defined window of development in early life is required for skin immune cell homeostasis and mediating tolerance to commensal bacteria (11,12). In aging individuals, physiological changes to the skin are concomitant with changes to the microbiome and a loss of phylogenetic diversity (13) (Fig. 1).
